opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important habits a researcher can build. Before I run something, I try to write down, even just in my head, what I expect to happen and why. The reason is simple: if you don't make a prediction, you can't really be surprised, and surprise is where you learn.

If the result matches your prediction, that's good. Your mental model of the system is roughly right, and you can move faster because you trust your intuition a bit more. But if the result doesn't match, that's even more valuable. It tells you something in your understanding is off. Maybe there's a bug, maybe the data isn't what you thought, or maybe there's a genuinely interesting phenomenon you didn't anticipate. Without a prior prediction, you'd just look at the number, say "okay," and move on. You'd miss the signal.

There's also a practical side. In deep learning, experiments are expensive. They take GPUs, time, sometimes weeks. If you can predict outcomes reasonably well, you can skip experiments whose results you already know and spend your compute on the ones where you're genuinely uncertain. That's where the information is.

And over time it trains your intuition, your research taste. Many people treat research like a slot machine: run a hundred configurations and see what comes out. But the people I admire most can reason about a system before touching it. Their predictions get sharper over the years because they keep checking themselves against reality. So for me, predicting the result is less about being right and more about keeping an honest loop between what I think I understand and what the world actually tells me.

r001.rationale: It says a matching result suggests the mental model is roughly right and builds trust in the intuition behind it, supporting continued use of that reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says a mismatch signals that something in the researcher’s understanding is off and may reveal a bug, bad data assumptions, or an unexpected phenomenon, prompting diagnosis of the discrepancy.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most underrated habits in research. Before you launch a run, you write down—sometimes literally in a notebook—what you expect the curve to look like, what number you think you'll get, and why. Then you run it.

The reason it matters is that an experiment only teaches you something relative to your prior. If you had no prediction, then whatever comes out, you'll find a way to rationalize it afterward. Humans are very good at that. The result goes up, you say "of course, the inductive bias helped." It goes down, you say "of course, it's overparameterized." Either way you feel like you understood it, but you didn't actually update your model of the world. If you committed to a prediction first, a wrong guess becomes a real signal. That gap between what you expected and what happened is where the actual learning is.

The second reason is more practical. Compute is finite, and students in particular tend to run things because they can, not because they should. If you force yourself to predict the outcome and you're very confident, maybe you don't need to run it at all, or you run a much smaller version. If you genuinely can't predict it, that's the experiment worth spending GPUs on. So prediction becomes a kind of filter for which experiments carry information.

And over time it builds intuition in a way that's hard to get otherwise. Early in my career I was wrong a lot. Things I thought would obviously help didn't, things I dismissed turned out to matter. Keeping track of that, almost like a calibration score, is how you eventually develop taste—the ability to look at an idea and have a feel for whether it will work. The people I consider really strong researchers are the ones whose predictions are right more often than chance, and the only way to get there is to make the predictions explicitly and get punished when you're wrong.

r001.rationale: The response says accurate predictions help build research intuition, but it does not explain that they support pursuing the line of reasoning that produced them.

r002.rationale: It describes a wrong prediction as a signal for learning, but does not say to examine where the reasoning behind that prediction went wrong.

astra-6.text:
I think making a prediction forces you to clarify what you actually believe. Before running an experiment, you should have some hypothesis about what will happen and why. Otherwise, it’s very easy to see the result and come up with a story afterward: “Oh, of course, that makes sense.” But that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve learned anything.

If you write down your prediction first, then the experiment becomes a test of your understanding. When the result is different, that’s especially interesting. What assumption was wrong? What did you miss? That gap can point you toward the next experiment. So the goal isn’t to be right every time. It’s to make it easier to recognize when your understanding needs to change.

r001.rationale: The response says a prediction tests your understanding, but does not explain that a correct prediction supports pursuing the reasoning that led to it.

r002.rationale: It says a different result prompts you to ask which assumption was wrong or what you missed, examining the reasoning behind the prediction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think making a prediction forces you to be explicit about your understanding. Before you run an experiment, you should ask: What do I expect to happen, and why? Otherwise, it’s very easy to see the result and come up with a story afterward that makes it seem obvious.

If the result matches your prediction, that gives you some confidence in your reasoning. But if it doesn’t, that’s often more interesting, because it reveals something you didn’t understand. You can then ask which assumption was wrong. So the point isn’t to be good at guessing results. It’s to make the experiment a way to improve your understanding, rather than just collect numbers.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that a result matching the prediction gives confidence in the reasoning, supporting continued pursuit of that line of thought.

r002.rationale: The candidate says a mismatch reveals something not understood and prompts asking which assumption was wrong.
